items.prompt:
Read this paragraph. Identify TWO problems (one off-topic sentence, one weak/vague sentence) and rewrite the entire paragraph fixing both.

'The Great Barrier Reef is in Australia. It is the biggest coral reef in the world. I want to go scuba diving someday. Lots of animals live in it. It is cool.'
items.answer: Off-topic: 'I want to go scuba diving someday.' Vague: 'It is cool.' Revised: 'The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef system, stretching over 1,400 miles along the northeastern coast of Australia. It is home to more than 1,500 species of fish, 4,000 types of mollusk, and hundreds of species of coral. Scientists study the reef to understand ocean ecosystems and the impacts of climate change on marine life. The Great Barrier Reef is one of the most extraordinary and biodiverse places on Earth — and one of the most important to protect.'

steps: Problem 1: Remove 'I want to go scuba diving someday' (personal wish, off-topic).
Problem 2: Replace 'It is cool' with a specific, informative concluding sentence.
Add a specific fact to strengthen the paragraph.

items.prompt:
A student wrote this narrative and received the peer feedback: 'Your story jumps from one event to another without any connections or feelings.' Identify TWO specific revision strategies this student should use, and rewrite the paragraph applying both.

'We went to the beach. I swam. I got sunburned. We drove home.'
items.answer: Revision strategy 1: Add temporal words and details to connect events. Revision strategy 2: Add character feelings. Revised: 'Last August, my family drove to the shore for the first time all summer, and the second I smelled the salty air, every worry I had left my mind. First, I ran straight into the waves without even taking off my sneakers, laughing at how cold and strong the water was. Then I spent two hours bodysurfing until I was too tired and too pink to stay in the sun any longer. Finally, exhausted and sunburned but completely happy, I fell asleep in the back seat before we had even left the parking lot.'

steps: Add temporal words: First, Then, Finally.
Add feelings: left my mind, laughing, exhausted but completely happy.
Add sensory details: salty air, cold and strong water, pink from sun.

items.prompt:
Read this student's opinion piece. Identify THREE specific problems and describe how to fix each. Then write the improved piece.

'I think every school should have a garden. Gardens are good. Also gardens are nice. My mom likes gardening. That is why gardens are good.'
items.answer: Problem 1: 'Gardens are good' and 'gardens are nice' are vague — no 'because' and no specific reasons. Problem 2: 'My mom likes gardening' is off-topic. Problem 3: The concluding sentence repeats the first sentence without adding anything new. Improved: 'I believe that every school should have a garden. School gardens are wonderful because they give students a hands-on way to learn about science, nutrition, and the environment. Also, gardens teach students responsibility because each child has to care for their plants, water them, and watch them grow over many weeks. For these reasons, a school garden is one of the best investments a school can make in its students.'

steps: Fix vague reasons by adding 'because' and specific benefits.
Remove the off-topic sentence about mom.
Replace the repeated closing with a strong, distinct concluding sentence.

items.prompt: A peer reviewer wrote this feedback on a student's informative paragraph: 'Your concluding sentence just repeats your introduction. Try wrapping up with a statement about why this topic matters.' Write an example of a weak concluding sentence and then a strong replacement for an informative paragraph about earthquakes.
items.answer: Weak concluding sentence: 'So that is what earthquakes are.' Strong concluding sentence: 'Understanding how earthquakes form and knowing how to prepare for them can mean the difference between safety and disaster for millions of people who live in earthquake-prone regions.'

steps: Weak: just restates the intro.
Strong: explains the significance, the real-world impact, or what the reader should take away.

items.prompt:
Read this narrative. A teacher says: 'Identify and fix the problem with focus, the weak ending, and one vague sentence.'

'I got a new bike for my birthday. It was red and shiny. I ate a big piece of cake. I rode it down the street and felt free. I went home happy.'
items.answer: Problem with focus: 'I ate a big piece of cake' is off-topic (the story is about the new bike, not the birthday party). Weak ending: 'I went home happy' has no reflection or specific feeling. Vague sentence: 'I rode it down the street and felt free' — good idea but vague about the actual experience. Revised: 'I got a new red bike for my birthday and could barely wait until everyone left to take it out. The bike was so shiny I could almost see my face in the paint. First, I walked it to the top of our street, my heart pounding. Then I pushed off, and as I coasted down the hill with the wind hitting my face and my hair flying out behind me, I understood exactly what freedom felt like. When I finally skidded to a stop at the bottom of the block, I thought I could have ridden all the way to the horizon and never stopped.'

steps: Remove off-topic sentence (birthday cake).
Replace weak ending with reflection.
Add specific sensory detail to 'felt free.'

items.prompt:
Write the PEER FEEDBACK a good reader would give for this paragraph. Your feedback must be specific, name the exact problem(s), and suggest at least one concrete revision.

'Wolves are interesting animals. They live in packs. My aunt visited a wolf sanctuary. Wolves howl to communicate. Wolves are cool.'
items.answer: Sample peer feedback: 'Your paragraph has some great facts about wolves, but there are two things to fix. First, the sentence about your aunt visiting a wolf sanctuary is off-topic — the paragraph is about wolves in general, not personal experiences. You should remove it. Second, the concluding sentence 'Wolves are cool' is too vague. Try replacing it with a sentence that explains why wolves are important, like: "Wolves play a vital role in their ecosystems by keeping deer and elk populations in balance, which helps forests and grasslands stay healthy."'

steps: Good peer feedback: names the specific problem, explains why it is a problem, and offers a concrete suggestion for improvement.

items.prompt:
Below is a student's first-draft narrative. Apply ALL of the following revisions: (1) remove the off-topic sentence, (2) add two temporal words, (3) strengthen the ending.

'We went hiking. We saw a waterfall. I have a new water bottle. The waterfall was loud. We sat and rested there.'
items.answer: Revised: 'Last Saturday, my family laced up our boots and set off on the hardest trail in the state park. First, we hiked for about two miles through thick forest, sweating and stopping every so often to drink from our water bottles. Then the trail opened up and we heard it before we saw it — a roar like thunder that grew louder with every step. The waterfall crashed over a wall of black rock and the cold mist hit our faces like a welcome breeze. Finally, we sat on a boulder near the base and rested in silence, listening to the water and feeling like we were the only people in the world.'

steps: Remove 'I have a new water bottle' (off-topic).
Add 'First' and 'Then' as temporal words.
Replace 'We sat and rested there' with a specific ending that includes sensory detail and a reflection.

items.prompt:
Compare these two revision strategies. For a paragraph about volcanoes, which is the BETTER revision strategy and why?

Strategy 1: Read the paragraph and change every adjective to a more interesting one.
Strategy 2: Read the paragraph for focus, then check that each sentence supports the main idea, then look for vague sentences to strengthen with specific details.
items.answer: Strategy 2 is better because it is systematic and targets the most important issues first: focus and relevance of each sentence, then quality of details. Strategy 1 only changes adjectives and ignores bigger issues like off-topic sentences or missing details. Good revision goes from big-picture issues (is every sentence on topic? is the main idea clear?) down to smaller improvements (word choice, detail).

steps: Effective revision prioritizes: (1) big-picture issues (topic focus, order, completeness), then (2) sentence-level improvements (vagueness, detail).
Changing only adjectives is a minor edit that does not address major weaknesses.

items.prompt:
A student's informative paragraph about Martin Luther King Jr. contains these sentences. Rank them from STRONGEST (1) to WEAKEST (4) and explain each ranking.

A) 'Martin Luther King Jr. was an important person.'
B) 'Dr. King was a civil rights leader who fought for equal rights for African Americans through peaceful protest during the 1950s and 1960s.'
C) 'He gave a famous speech called "I Have a Dream" in 1963, which called on America to live up to its promise that all people are created equal.'
D) 'Dr. King is famous.'
items.answer: Ranking: 1 (strongest) = C — specific event, title, year, and meaning of the speech. 2 = B — clear factual description with context. 3 = A — at least it names the topic, but 'important person' is too vague. 4 (weakest) = D — provides no information at all.

steps: C is strongest: most specific (date, speech title, content and significance).
B is second: gives factual context.
A is third: correct but vague.
D is weakest: adds no information.

items.prompt:
Read this paragraph and identify the BEST single revision that would most improve it. Explain your reasoning.

'Rain falls from clouds. Rain is water. It helps plants grow. Rain falls a lot in some places.'
items.answer: Best revision: replace the vague sentences with specific facts and add a concluding sentence that explains why rain matters. For example, replace 'Rain is water' with a definition: 'Rain is precipitation that forms when water droplets in clouds grow heavy enough to fall to Earth.' This is the most impactful single change because giving a definition transforms the vaguest sentence into the most informative one, and it models how the other sentences should also be strengthened.

steps: The weakest and most easily improved sentence is 'Rain is water' — it is technically true but provides zero new information.
Replacing it with a definition/explanation turns a vague statement into the backbone of an informative paragraph.

items.prompt: Write a checklist of FIVE revision questions a Grade 2 student should ask before turning in any piece of writing. Explain each question briefly.
items.answer: 1. Is every sentence on my topic? (Remove anything that does not connect to the main idea.) 2. Are my reasons or facts specific? (Replace vague words like 'good' or 'nice' with 'because' and details.) 3. Does my beginning introduce the topic clearly? (Check that the first sentence sets up the piece.) 4. Does my ending wrap up the piece? (Make sure the last sentence gives closure, not just 'The End.') 5. Did I add details that help the reader picture or understand? (Look for any sentence that could be made more vivid or specific.)

steps: Each revision question should address a different aspect: focus, detail, opening, closing, and vividness.

items.prompt:
Read this opinion piece. A teacher says it has two separate problems: one sentence that hurts the writer's argument, and one place where a reason is asserted but not explained. Identify both and write the revised piece.

'I think homework should be shorter. Homework takes a long time. Also, I don't like homework. That is why homework should be shorter.'
items.answer: Problem 1: 'Also, I don't like homework' hurts the argument — it sounds like a complaint, not a reason, and makes the writer seem biased. Problem 2: 'Homework takes a long time' asserts a claim without explaining WHY that is a problem. Revised: 'I think homework should be shorter. Long homework assignments take too much time because students often have other responsibilities after school, such as sports, family chores, or reading for fun. Shorter homework is more effective because students can focus on the most important skills without feeling overwhelmed or burned out. That is why I believe a small amount of meaningful homework is better than a large amount that leaves students exhausted.'

steps: Remove/replace the complaint ('I don't like homework') with a logical reason.
Expand 'Homework takes a long time' with 'because' and a specific explanation.

items.prompt:
Write a REVISION of the following narrative to make it stronger. You must: add at least two temporal words, remove the off-topic sentence, add a character feeling, and improve the ending.

'I lost my library book. I looked everywhere. I love chocolate ice cream. I found it under the couch. I gave it back.'
items.answer: Revised: 'One morning, I reached into my backpack to get my library book and felt nothing but empty air — my stomach dropped when I realized it was gone. First, I searched my whole room, pulling back blankets and looking under the bed. Then I checked the living room, tossing couch cushions aside until, finally, my fingers closed around the worn cover tucked all the way against the back wall. Relieved and a little embarrassed, I tucked it safely into my bag and promised myself I would always put it in the same spot from now on.'

steps: Remove 'I love chocolate ice cream' (off-topic).
Add temporal words: First, Then, Finally.
Add feeling: stomach dropped, relieved.
Improve ending: add a reflection or lesson learned.

items.prompt: A teacher returns a student's informative paragraph with this comment: 'Your paragraph has good facts, but your concluding sentence does not add anything new — it just says the same thing as your introduction. Revise your concluding sentence.' The introduction was: 'Sharks are amazing ocean animals.' The student's concluding sentence was: 'Sharks are really amazing ocean animals.' Write a stronger concluding sentence.
items.answer: Strong concluding sentence: 'Despite their fearsome reputation, sharks are essential to healthy oceans — and understanding them is the first step to protecting both these remarkable animals and the ecosystems they help maintain.'

steps: A strong concluding sentence: does not repeat the introduction, adds a new idea (significance, consequence, call to action), and uses formal language.

items.prompt:
Apply all revision steps to this paragraph. Identify every problem and write the fully revised version.

'Dogs are nice pets. They have fur. I think all people should have a dog. My grandma has three cats. Dogs can do tricks. Dogs are the best.'
items.answer: Problems: (1) 'nice pets' and 'Dogs are the best' are vague opinions without support. (2) 'My grandma has three cats' is off-topic. (3) 'I think all people should have a dog' unexpectedly switches to opinion in an informative paragraph. (4) 'Dogs can do tricks' is vague. Revised informative version: 'Dogs are loyal and intelligent animals that have lived alongside humans for thousands of years. They have a thick coat of fur that comes in hundreds of colors and patterns, from the sleek golden coat of a Labrador to the curly hair of a poodle. Dogs are highly trainable and can learn commands that help them work as service animals, search-and-rescue partners, and therapy companions. Their intelligence, loyalty, and adaptability make dogs one of the most remarkable animals in the world.'

steps: Remove opinion sentences.
Remove off-topic sentence.
Strengthen vague sentences with specific details.
Concluding sentence: wrap up with the qualities that make dogs remarkable.
